newsitem.title: UK: British unemployment falls to 17-year low. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: British unemployment falls to 17-year low. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]

text.p: The number of unemployed in Britain fell to a 17-year low in July, indicating a further strengthening of the domestic economy, according to data released on Wednesday.
The jobless report sent prices on financial markets lower, as investors worried about the inflationary impact of strong economic growth.
But these concerns were partly tempered by figures showing growth in British wages had held steady in June.

A separate report from the Bank of England said the central bank had held back from raising interest rates by 1/2 rather than 1/4 point in July because the sharper increase could have pushed up the pound unnecessarily.
The jobless total fell by a larger-than-expected 49,800 to 1.55 million in July, its lowest level since September 1980.
Economists had forecast a drop of 31,000.
The unemployment rate fell to 5.5 percent from 5.7 percent in June.
The evidence of a stronger economy worried markets because of the possibility of more rises in interest rates, after four rate hikes already in just four months.
The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares dropped on the news, falling to 5,021.9 points, a drop of around 50 points or one percent on the day.
Government bond prices also dipped, with the key September gilts contract down 18/32 to 114-06.

Some economists appeared less worried about the jobless fall, pointing instead to the other figures released on Wednesday showing steady growth in average earnings of 4.25 (corrects from 4.5) percent in June.
The currency markets also homed in on the earnings figures and sterling eased back on what traders said was positive news for inflation from the earnings report.
British Education and Employment Minister Baroness Blackstone welcomed the fall in the overall jobless total but said long-term youth unemployment remained a problem.
But she too pointed to the earnings figures which she called "particularly encouraging".
Publishing the minutes of its July 9-10 monetary policy committee meeting, the Bank of England said there had been a unanimous vote for an immediate rise of 1/4 point in interest rates.
The BoE raised interest rates by another 1/4 point to 7.0 percent last week, prompting speculation that interest rates may now have peaked for the time being.
The committee said that in July it had discussed the relative merits of a rise in rates of a quarter point or a half point.

It said said there was a risk that an increase of a half point would lead to an upward revision of the expected level at which interest rates would peak and would cause the exchange rate to appreciate unnecessarily.
